claims.text: Smaller FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles exhibit lower apparent thermal stability than larger nanoparticles.
Increased surface-energy effects in smaller nanoparticles promote an earlier onset of melting.
Increased surface-energy effects in smaller nanoparticles promote earlier morphological changes.
The FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles are synthesized with controlled size distributions.
A controlled thermal ramp on an in-situ heating stage can be used to study the nanoparticles' thermal response.
High-vacuum or inert-atmosphere heating minimizes oxidation of the nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a higher surface-to-volume ratio.
A higher surface-to-volume ratio enhances the influence of surface energy.
In smaller FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles, the increased surface-energy contribution lowers the effective melting or transformation temperature.
The increased surface-energy contribution destabilizes the crystalline structure of smaller FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles.
Under identical heating conditions, smaller FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles undergo phase changes earlier than larger particles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles will begin melting or coalescing at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Larger FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles maintain structural stability to higher temperatures because their relative surface-energy contribution is lower.
In-situ transmission electron microscopy with a heating stage can monitor size-dependent morphological and phase changes in FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles during heating.
Changes in TEM diffraction patterns can indicate phase transformation during heating.
